title: Waging War on the Bad Guys
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart, returning from Common Core workshops in Oklahoma and Missouri with 300 feedback forms in hand, borrows a podcaster's frame: serving people in a niche means naming the dragons and forging swords to kill them. He first narrows the field to problems teachers can actually influence, contrasting the classroom, where the teacher is the greatest influencer, with complaints like the public's low opinion of teachers, which only worsen with whining. The first dragon is the flood of mediocre 'Common Core aligned' resources, where anyone can slap a sticker on a textbook or Teachers Pay Teachers lesson and whole districts get fooled. His sword against it is the non-freaked-out approach: pick the highest-leverage standards, internalize them and build resources that fit the local setting rather than buying compliance. The second dragon is mediocre professional development, and he spreads the blame evenly, needling teachers who would dismiss Jesus himself as a PD presenter while also faulting PD decisions made without empowered teachers. He closes with concrete demands on both sides: less talking at audiences, more active practice and more teacher-administrator collaboration about what PD is needed.
points: Stuart's filter for which problems deserve energy is influence: he focuses on what a teacher controls and dismisses grievances, like public opinion of teachers, that worsen the more they are voiced.

He treats 'Common Core aligned' labels as fool's gold, citing Michael McShane's point that anyone can put the sticker on a product, so districts can believe they are aligning when they are only enriching vendors.

His alternative to buying alignment is teacher-built alignment: choose the biggest-bang standards, learn them deeply and create resources for the specific setting, which also builds a common cross-content language.
On professional development he refuses a one-sided indictment, arguing that teachers' own graceless reception of PD is part of the problem alongside decisions made without teacher input.
His prescription for better PD is structural - less lecture, more interaction and processing, more practice, and joint teacher-administrator planning of what PD a school actually needs.
quotes: And before I share who the bad guys are in my opinion, let me just state that I love focusing on problems I can tackle, and I despise focusing on problems I can't touch.
At the same time, I hate focusing on problems like “the public has a low opinion of teachers.” It's one of those problems where, the more you whine about it the worse it's actually going to get.

As McShane points out, anyone can put a Common Core sticker on a textbook or a Teachers Pay Teachers lesson. The resulting over-abundance of non-Common-Core-aligned “Common Core aligned” stuff is a veritable nightmare.
It's simple. It's proven. It empowers teachers with a working knowledge of the Core.

And let's be honest: part of this is our fault as teachers. I swear that, for some of my friends, if Jesus himself walked in and led a professional development session, the second he was done they'd be like, “Well, that's easy for him to say — he's retired.
I'm not saying any of this is easy; I'm just saying it's something we have the power to influence. It's a dragon we can make swords for.
